facts.statement: The animal belongs to the genus Barosaurus.
facts.quote: genus: Barosaurus

facts.statement: The only valid species is Barosaurus lentus.
facts.quote: species: lentus

facts.statement: Barosaurus affinis is considered a synonym of Barosaurus lentus.
facts.quote: synonyms: *Barosaurus affinis Marsh, 1899

facts.statement: Barosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1890.
facts.quote: It was described by American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh in 1890.

facts.statement: Barosaurus lived in present-day North America during the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Barosaurus ( ) ("heavy lizard") is a genus of large sauropod dinosaur that lived in present-day North America during the Late Jurassic period.

facts.statement: Barosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, approximately 152 to 150 million years ago.
facts.quote: Barosaurus is known from the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic period, which dates to around 152 to 150 million years ago.

facts.statement: Adult Barosaurus measured about 25 to 27 meters in length and weighed between 12 and 20 metric tons.
facts.quote: Barosaurus was an enormous animal, with some adults measuring about 25 - 27 m in length and weighing about 12–20 metric tons (13–22 short tons).

facts.statement: Compared to Diplodocus, Barosaurus had a relatively longer neck but a shorter tail.
facts.quote: In comparison to its close kin Diplodocus, Barosaurus has a relatively longer neck but shorter tail.

facts.statement: Barosaurus possessed 16 cervical vertebrae, which are more numerous than those of Diplodocus and Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Barosaurus has 16 cervical vertebrae, more than Diplodocus and Apatosaurus, which are extremely elongated.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of B. lentus initially consisted of four tail vertebrae found in 1889 in South Dakota by Isabella R. Ellerman.
facts.quote: B. lentus holotype (name-bearing) specimen initially consisted of four caudal (tail) vertebrae that were found in 1889 in South Dakota by Ms. Isabella R. Ellerman.

facts.statement: Specimens of Barosaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation in Utah and Montana, with potential fossils reported from Colorado, Wyoming, and Oklahoma.
facts.quote: Several other specimens have been collected outcrops of the Morrison Formation in Utah and Montana, though fossils potentially from the genus have been reported from Colorado, Wyoming, and Oklahoma as well.

facts.statement: The first Barosaurus remains were discovered in 1889 in the Morrison Formation of South Dakota by Isabella R. Ellerman and excavated by Othniel Charles Marsh and John Bell Hatcher.
facts.quote: Initial discoveries The first Barosaurus remains were discovered in the Morrison Formation of South Dakota by Ms. Isabella R. Ellerman, postmistress of Postville, and excavated by Othniel Charles Marsh and John Bell Hatcher of Yale University in 1889.

facts.statement: Four neck vertebrae, each 1 meter long, were collected in 1912 and later identified as belonging to Barosaurus by William Jacob Holland.
facts.quote: Four neck vertebrae, each 1 meter (3 feet) long, were collected in 1912 near a specimen of Diplodocus, but a few years later, William Jacob Holland realized they belonged to a different species.

facts.statement: In 1929, Barnum Brown arranged for the most complete Barosaurus specimen to be moved to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City.
facts.quote: However, in 1929 Barnum Brown arranged for all of the material to be shipped to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, where it remains today.

facts.statement: The Morrison Formation environment where Barosaurus lived featured a floodplain with hot summers and moderate winters.
facts.quote: The Morrison Formation had a floodplain environment with hot summers and moderate winters.

facts.statement: It is noted that late 20th-century depictions of Barosaurus as a short-tailed sauropod with a U-shaped neck are considered errors based on a specific artistic interpretation.
facts.quote: Darren Naish has noted a common error in books of the late 20th century to depict Barosaurus as a kind of brachiosaur-like short tailed sauropod with raphes on its neck and body, and often curving the upper half of its neck downwards into a U-shape, citing it as an example of a Palaeoart meme.

facts.statement: Paleontologist David Evans discovered a reference to a Barosaurus skeleton in the Royal Ontario Museum collection in 2007.
facts.quote: In 2007, the newly appointed curator of the ROM, paleontologist David Evans, was flying to the U.S. Badlands when he discovered a literature reference to a Barosaurus skeleton in the ROM collection.

facts.statement: The Royal Ontario Museum Barosaurus specimen is nicknamed "Gordo" after curator Gordon Edmunds.
facts.quote: The ROM specimen is nicknamed "Gordo" after Gordon Edmunds, the museum curator who arranged for the skeleton to be brought to the ROM.

facts.statement: The Royal Ontario Museum Barosaurus specimen is about 40% complete and wears a Diplodocus skull because no Barosaurus skull has ever been found.
facts.quote: The specimen is about 40% complete, but as a skull of Barosaurus has never been found, the ROM specimen wears the head of a Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Eberhard Fraas discovered sauropod skeletons in the Tendaguru Beds of German East Africa (now Tanzania) in 1907.
facts.quote: Misidentified discoveries in Africa In 1907, German paleontologist Eberhard Fraas discovered the skeletons of two sauropods on an expedition to the Tendaguru Beds in German East Africa (now Tanzania).

facts.statement: The genus name Gigantosaurus was preoccupied, leading to the reclassification of Fraas's African sauropods into the genus Tornieria in 1911.
facts.quote: However, this genus name had already been given to the fragmentary remains of a sauropod from England. Both species were moved to a new genus, Tornieria, in 1911.

facts.statement: Werner Janensch reclassified the African sauropod species into the genus Barosaurus after studying fossils from the Tendaguru Beds.
facts.quote: Upon further study of these remains and many other sauropod fossils from the hugely productive Tendaguru Beds, Werner Janensch moved the species once again, this time to the North American genus Barosaurus.

facts.statement: In 1991, Gigantosaurus robustus was recognized as a titanosaur and placed in the new genus Janenschia.
facts.quote: In 1991, "Gigantosaurus" robustus was recognized as a titanosaur and placed in a new genus, Janenschia, as J. robusta.

facts.statement: The African sauropod species, once thought to be Barosaurus africanus, is now classified as Tornieria africana.
facts.quote: The African species, although closely related to Barosaurus lentus and Diplodocus from North America, is now once again known as Tornieria africana.

facts.statement: It is debated whether a specimen from the Kadsi Formation in Zimbabwe represents Barosaurus, as its referral is doubtful due to poor preservation and it may instead be Tornieria.
facts.quote: A species of Barosaurus was also allegedly identified from the Kadsi Formation in Zimbabwe in 1987. However, this material is poorly preserved and fragmentary and was not adequately diagnosed as such, and so its referral to Barosaurus is doubtful. It may represent Tornieria.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had a longer neck and shorter tail than Diplodocus but was about the same overall length.
facts.quote: Barosaurus was differently proportioned than its close relative Diplodocus, with a longer neck and shorter tail, but was about the same length overall.

facts.statement: Barosaurus was longer than Apatosaurus but had a less robust skeleton.
facts.quote: It was longer than Apatosaurus, but its skeleton was less robust.

facts.statement: Most distinguishing features of Barosaurus are found in the vertebrae, though a complete vertebral column has never been discovered.
facts.quote: Most of the distinguishing skeletal features of Barosaurus were in the vertebrae, although a complete vertebral column has never been found.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had only 9 dorsal vertebrae, whereas Diplodocus and Apatosaurus had 10.
facts.quote: Diplodocus and Apatosaurus both had 15 cervical (neck) and 10 dorsal (trunk) vertebrae, while Barosaurus had only 9 dorsals.

facts.statement: A dorsal vertebra may have been converted into a cervical one, resulting in a total of 16 neck vertebrae in Barosaurus.
facts.quote: A dorsal may have been converted into a cervical vertebra, for a total of 16 vertebrae in the neck.

facts.statement: The neural spines on Barosaurus vertebrae were not as tall or complex as those in Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The neural spines protruding from the top of the vertebrae were neither as tall or as complex in Barosaurus as they were in Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Barosaurus tail chevrons were forked with a prominent forward spike, similar to Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The chevron bones lining the underside of the tail were forked and had a prominent forward spike, much like the closely related Diplodocus.

facts.statement: The Barosaurus tail likely ended in a long whiplash, similar to other diplodocids which could have up to 80 tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The tail probably ended in a long whiplash, much like Apatosaurus, Diplodocus and other diplodocids, some of which had up to 80 tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had limb bones that were virtually indistinguishable from those of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The limb bones of Barosaurus were virtually indistinguishable from those of Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Barosaurus was a quadruped with columnar limbs adapted to support its enormous bulk.
facts.quote: Both were quadrupedal, with columnar limbs adapted to support the enormous bulk of the animals.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had a single carpal bone in its wrist and more slender metacarpals than Diplodocus.
facts.quote: There was a single carpal bone in the wrist, and the metacarpals were more slender than those of Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Although Barosaurus feet have never been discovered, it is believed to have been digitigrade with five small toes on each foot.
facts.quote: Barosaurus feet have never been discovered, but like other sauropods, it would have been digitigrade, with all four feet each bearing five small toes.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had a large claw on the inside digit of its forefoot and smaller claws on the inside three digits of its hindfoot.
facts.quote: A large claw adorned the inside digit on the manus (forefoot) while smaller claws tipped the inside three digits of the pes (hindfoot).

facts.statement: Barosaurus is a member of the sauropod family Diplodocidae and is sometimes placed in the subfamily Diplodocinae with Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Barosaurus is a member of the sauropod family Diplodocidae, and sometimes placed with Diplodocus in the subfamily Diplodocinae.

facts.statement: Tornieria and Australodocus from the Tendaguru Beds of Tanzania in eastern Africa have been classified as diplodocines.
facts.quote: Tornieria (formerly "Barosaurus" africanus) and Australodocus from the famous Tendaguru Beds of Tanzania in eastern Africa have also been classified as diplodocines.

facts.statement: Diplodocid fossils, including those of Barosaurus, are found in North America, Europe, and Africa.
facts.quote: Diplodocid fossils are found in North America, Europe, and Africa.

facts.statement: A 2016 preprint by Mike Taylor and Mathew Wedel argued that Barosaurus cervical vertebrae allowed significant lateral neck flexibility but restricted vertical flexibility.
facts.quote: In a 2016 preprint, Mike Taylor and Mathew Wedel argued that the structure of the cervical vertebrae of Barosaurus allowed for a significant degree of lateral flexibility in the neck, but restricted vertical flexibility.

facts.statement: The restriction in vertical neck flexibility suggests Barosaurus did not primarily feed on vegetation high off the ground.
facts.quote: The restriction in vertical flexibility suggests that Barosaurus did not primarily feed on vegetation that was high off the ground.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding sauropod posture, with traditional views depicting a sprawled gait and later studies suggesting necks held high to graze tall trees.
facts.quote: While diplodocids were traditionally depicted as having a sprawled, lizard-like gait, later studies often portrayed them with their necks held high up in the air, allowing them to graze from tall trees.

facts.statement: Studies conclude that the neutral posture of Diplodocus was close to horizontal, leading scientists like Kent Stevens to argue that Barosaurus did not raise its head much above shoulder level.
facts.quote: Studies looking at the morphology of sauropod necks have concluded that the neutral posture of Barosaurus' close relative Diplodocus neck was close to horizontal, rather than vertical, and scientists such as Kent Stevens have used this to argue that sauropods including Barosaurus did not raise their heads much above shoulder level.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that a nuchal ligament may have held Barosaurus' neck in a horizontal position.
facts.quote: A nuchal ligament may have held the neck in this position.

facts.statement: Another hypothesis suggests Barosaurus possessed an avian-like elastic ligament similar to that seen in Struthio camelus.
facts.quote: Another hypothesized neck-supporting ligament is an avian-like elastic ligament, such as that seen in Struthio camelus.

facts.statement: A 2009 study argued that sauropods likely held their necks at maximum vertical extension in an alert posture, unless unique soft tissue anatomy differed from other animals.
facts.quote: A 2009 study found that all tetrapods appear to hold the base of their necks at the maximum possible vertical extension when in a normal, alert posture, and argued that the same would hold true for sauropods barring any unknown, unique characteristics that set the soft tissue anatomy of their necks apart from other animals.

facts.statement: The idea that diplodocoids held their necks vertically might be contradicted by evidence that their inner ears are aligned for a horizontal neck pose.
facts.quote: However, this idea might be contradicted due to the inner ear of diplodocoids actually being in alignment for a horizontal neck pose.

facts.statement: The extremely long neck of Barosaurus is a subject of significant scientific controversy.
facts.quote: The very long neck of Barosaurus is the source of much controversy among scientists.

facts.statement: A 1992 study suggested that Barosaurus would have needed a heart weighing 1.6 tons, which is about one-tenth of its body weight, to pump blood up its long neck.
facts.quote: A 1992 Columbia University study of diplodocid neck structure indicated that the longest necks would have required a 1.6-ton heart – a tenth of the animal's body weight.

facts.statement: Some researchers argue that Barosaurus held its head and neck in a near-horizontal posture, which would have made blood supply to the brain easier.
facts.quote: Some argue that the near-horizontal posture of the head and neck would have eliminated the problem of supplying blood to the brain, as it would not be elevated.

facts.statement: Barosaurus fossils are found in sediments dating to the late Kimmeridgian to early Tithonian stages, approximately 150 million years ago.
facts.quote: Barosaurus fossils are found in late Kimmeridgian to early Tithonian sediments, around 150 million years old.

facts.statement: Barosaurus lived in an environment dominated by other giant sauropods including Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, and Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: The Morrison Formation records an environment and time dominated by gigantic sauropod dinosaurs such as Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus and Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: Barosaurus shared its habitat with herbivorous ornithischians like Camptosaurus and Stegosaurus, and theropod predators such as Allosaurus and Saurophaganax.
facts.quote: Dinosaurs that lived alongside Barosaurus included the herbivorous ornithischians Camptosaurus, Dryosaurus, Stegosaurus and Othnielosaurus, and predators in this paleoenvironment included the theropods Saurophaganax, Allosaurus, Torvosaurus, Ceratosaurus, Marshosaurus, Stokesosaurus and Ornitholestes.

facts.statement: High atmospheric carbon dioxide levels during the Late Jurassic created a greenhouse effect with high global temperatures.
facts.quote: Very high atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide in the Late Jurassic led to high temperatures around the globe, due to the greenhouse effect.

facts.statement: One study estimated that Late Jurassic CO2 levels of 1120 ppm resulted in average winter temperatures of 20°C and summer temperatures of 40-45°C in western North America.
facts.quote: One study, estimating CO2 concentrations of 1120 parts per million, predicted average winter temperatures in western North America of 20 °C and summer temperatures averaging 40 - 45 C.

facts.statement: A more recent study suggested Late Jurassic CO2 concentrations could have reached up to 3180 parts per million.
facts.quote: A more recent study suggested even higher CO2 concentrations of up to 3180 parts per million.

facts.statement: The climate of Barosaurus's habitat was semi-arid with seasonal rainfall, caused by high evaporation and rain shadows from western mountains.
facts.quote: Warm temperatures that led to significant evaporation year-round, along with possible rain shadow effect from the mountains to the west, led to a semi-arid climate with only seasonal rainfall.

facts.quote: species_authority: Marsh, 1890

facts.statement: Barosaurus lentus is the only known species of the extinct genus Barosaurus, a diplodocid sauropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: Barosaurus lentus (gr. "lagarto pesado lento") es la única especie conocida del género extinto Barosaurus de dinosaurio saurópodo diplodócido

facts.statement: The name Barosaurus comes from the Greek words barys meaning 'heavy' and sauros meaning 'lizard'.
facts.quote: El término compuesto Barosaurus proviene de las palabras griegas barys, βαρυς que significa "pesado" y sauros σαυρος, que significa "lagarto".

facts.statement: The American Museum of Natural History in New York possesses a Barosaurus skeleton posed with its mother standing on hind legs to protect her young from an Allosaurus.
facts.quote: El Museo Americano de Historia Natural en Nueva York, tiene un esqueleto de una madre Barosaurus parada en sus piernas traseras a una altura enorme para proteger a su prole contra un Allosaurus.

facts.statement: It is currently unknown whether Barosaurus could have stood in the posed position of a mother protecting her young in life.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, el que Barosaurus pudiera colocarse de tal manera en vida, es aún desconocido.

facts.statement: Barosaurus remains have been found in the Morrison Formation in Utah and South Dakota, and possibly in Africa as evidenced by the Kadisi Formation.
facts.quote: Los restos se han encontrado en la Formación Morrison en el Período Jurásico Superior en las zonas estratigráficas 2-5 de Utah y Dakota del Sur y posiblemente África, como lo demuestra la Formación Kadsi.

facts.statement: Barosaurus was a large but typical diplodocid with a long neck and a long whip-like tail.
facts.quote: Barosaurus era un diplodócido grande pero bastante típico con un cuello largo y una también larga cola en forma de látigo.

facts.statement: Some adult Barosaurus measured more than 26 meters in length and weighed more than 20 tonnes.
facts.quote: Barosaurus era un animal enorme, con algunos adultos que mide más de 26 metros de longitud y un peso de más de 20 toneladas.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had shorter caudal vertebrae than Diplodocus, resulting in a shorter tail.
facts.quote: Barosaurus tenía vértebras caudales en la cola más cortas que Diplodocus, resultando en una cola más corta.

facts.statement: The first Barosaurus remains were discovered in the Morrison Formation of South Dakota by Mrs. E.R. Ellerman and excavated by Othniel Charles Marsh and John Bell Hatcher in 1889.
facts.quote: Los primeros restos de Barosaurus fueron descubiertos en la Formación Morrison de Dakota del Sur por la Sra E.R. Ellerman, empleada de correos de Pottsville, y excavados por Othniel Charles Marsh y John Bell Hatcher de la Universidad de Yale en 1889.

facts.statement: Marsh named Barosaurus lentus, derived from Greek words meaning 'heavy' and 'lizard', and Latin meaning 'slow'.
facts.quote: Marsh nombró Barosaurus lentus, por los vocablos griegos βαρυς/barys ("pesado") y σαυρος/sauros ("lagarto"), y del latín lentus ("lento").

facts.statement: The type specimen of Barosaurus was fully described by Richard Swann Lull in 1919 after being prepared at Yale in the winter of 1917.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo de Barosaurus habían sido finalmente preparado en Yale en el invierno de 1917 y fue descrito completamente por Richard Swann Lull en 1919.

facts.statement: In 1929, Barnum Brown organized the material to be sent to the American Museum of Natural History in New York, where it remains today.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, en 1929 Barnum Brown organizó todo el material para ser enviado al Museo Americano de Historia Natural en Nueva York , donde permanece en la actualidad.

facts.statement: A vertebra interpreted as the northernmost record of Barosaurus lentus has been reported from the Pryor Mountains in Montana.
facts.quote: A vertebra interpreted as the northernmost record of Barosaurus lentus from the Morrison Formation reported to date is described from the Pryor Mountains (Montana, United States) by Woodruff et al. (2026).

facts.statement: Barosaurus was quadrupedal with pillar-like limbs adapted to support its enormous mass, similar to Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Los huesos de las extremidades de Barosaurus eran virtualmente indistinguibles de las de Diplodocus. Ambos eran cuadrúpedos, con extremidades con forma de columna adaptados para soportar la enorme masa de los animales.

facts.statement: Although Barosaurus feet have never been found, they likely were digitigrade with five small toes on each foot, like other sauropods.
facts.quote: Los pies de Barosaurus nunca han sido descubiertos, pero al igual que otros saurópodos, que habrían sido digitígrados, con las cuatro patas que llevan cada cinco pequeños dedos de los pies.

facts.statement: It was once hypothesized that Barosaurus had eight hearts to pump blood to its brain when holding its neck vertically, but this theory was discarded due to physiological inconsistencies.
facts.quote: Antiguamente se creía que Barosaurus podía levantar su largo cuello hacia arriba como una jirafa. Para bombear sangre al cerebro, el corazón habría tenido que pesar cerca de 1,6 toneladas. Cuanto más grande un corazón es, más lento el latido. Pero en ese caso, la sangre fluiría de nuevo al corazón antes de que alcanzara el cerebro. Debido a esta inconsistencia, existió una teoría radical que afirmaba que Barosaurus tenía 8 corazones, dos en el pecho y tres pares en el cuello.

facts.statement: Another theory suggested Barosaurus had arterial sphincters to reduce blood backflow, though this was later resolved by computer models showing horizontal neck posture.
facts.quote: Otra teoría postuló que tenía esfínteres arteriales que reducían la cantidad de sangre que retrocedía.

facts.statement: A 2026 study reported a pathology found in the whip section of a Barosaurus tail specimen.
facts.quote: van der Linden et al. (2026) report on a specimen of Barosaurus with a pathology in the "whip" part of the tail.

facts.quote: En 1898 fue clasificado por él por primera vez como un diplodócido.
